claims.text: The characteristic features of a text are the features that make it recognisably the kind of text it is — its conventions of form, its structural habits, its recurring language choices.

claims.text: The opening move of an analysis fixes the text’s form, audience, purpose and context in a sentence or two, because every feature discussed later is judged by what it does for them.

claims.text: Analysis is about how a text is written; responding to its topic — agreeing, arguing, explaining the subject — answers a different question and earns none of the analysis marks.

claims.text: A text’s overall style is the manner its choices produce together; it is characterised in two or three precise words and then proved through specific choices.

claims.text: A claim about style counts only when specific choices prove it; general adjectives with no example behind them leave the claim unsupported.

claims.text: Form covers the kind of text and its conventions; structure covers the organisation of the whole text — opening, sequence, shifts, paragraphing, ending; language covers the choices inside sentences.

claims.text: The structural features worth analysing in a non-fiction text are its opening and what it promises, its shifts of focus, its paragraph lengths, its sequence, its repetition across the text and its ending.

claims.text: Retelling or summarising the text, often at length, is not analysing it: content is mentioned only to anchor a point about a choice.

claims.text: Several choices can work together towards one effect, so the strongest analysis shows how a structural choice and a language choice support each other.

claims.text: Analysing features as a system means tracing their joint effect rather than listing them one by one; a text’s meaning is made by combinations, not by isolated devices.

claims.text: An effect is what a writer’s choice leads the reader to think, feel or do at that point in the text; it is not the same as what the words mean.

claims.text: The analytical sequence runs feature, evidence (the exact words), effect on this reader, link to the text’s purpose — four moves, in that order, until they are habit.

claims.text: Naming devices and sentence types without saying what any of them does is feature-spotting, and it earns little: the point is made only when the writer says what the choice does for this reader.

claims.text: An analysis organised by effect or purpose builds an argument about the whole text; one that follows the order of the text’s paragraphs tends to become a commentary on each in turn.

claims.text: The introduction of a text analysis states the text’s form, audience and purpose and names its overall manner in two or three precise words; the conclusion gathers the argument into a final view of what the text achieves for its reader.

claims.text: Working through the text paragraph by paragraph, or jumping around it with no line of argument, scatters the analysis: points about the same effect end up far apart and the answer never states a view.
